**The Doon School** (informally **Doon School** or **Doon**) is a [selective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selective_school "Selective school") all-boys [private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_school "Private school") boarding school in [Dehradun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehradun "Dehradun"), Uttarakhand, India, which was established in 1935. It was envisioned by [Satish Ranjan Das](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Ranjan_Das "Satish Ranjan Das"), a lawyer from [Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcutta "Calcutta"), as a school modelled on the British [public school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_school_(United_Kingdom) "Public school (United Kingdom)") while remaining conscious of Indian ambitions and desires. The school admitted its first pupils on 10 September 1935, and formally opened on 27 October 1935, with [Lord Willingdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Willingdon "Lord Willingdon") presiding over the ceremony. The school's first headmaster was [Arthur E. Foot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Foot "Arthur Foot"), an English educationalist who had spent nine years as a science master at [Eton College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eton_College "Eton College"), England.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-2)

The school houses roughly 580 pupils aged 12 to 18, and admission is based on a competitive entrance examination and an interview with the headmaster. Every year boys are admitted in only two-year groups: [seventh grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_grade "Seventh grade") in January and [eighth grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighth_grade "Eighth grade") in April. As of May 2019, boys from 26 [Indian states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_and_union_territories_of_India "States and union territories of India") as well as 35 [non-resident Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-resident_Indians "Non-resident Indians") and foreign nationals were studying at Doon.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-3) The school is fully residential, and boys and most teachers live on campus. In tenth grade, students take the [Cambridge IGCSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGCSE "IGCSE") examinations, and for the final two years can choose between the [Indian School Certificate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_School_Certificate "Indian School Certificate") or [International Baccalaureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Baccalaureate "International Baccalaureate"). A broad range of extra-curricular activities, numbering around 80, are offered to the boys, and early masters such as [R.L. Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R.L._Holdsworth "R.L. Holdsworth"), [J.A.K. Martyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J.A.K._Martyn "J.A.K. Martyn"), [Jack Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Gibson_(schoolmaster) "Jack Gibson (schoolmaster)") and [Gurdial Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurdial_Singh_(mountaineer) "Gurdial Singh (mountaineer)") established a strong tradition of [mountaineering at school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Role_of_The_Doon_School_in_Indian_mountaineering "Role of The Doon School in Indian mountaineering"). The school occupies the former site of the [Forest Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Research_Institute_(India) "Forest Research Institute (India)") and is home to diverse flora and fauna. Doon remains a boys-only school despite continued pressure from political leaders to become [coeducational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-sex_education "Mixed-sex education").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-4)[Old boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_boy_network "Old boy network") of the school are known as '[Doscos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Doon_School_alumni "List of The Doon School alumni")'.

Doon has been consistently ranked as the best all-boys residential school in India.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-5) Although the school has often been cited as 'Eton of India' by media outlets such as the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-6)_[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-7)_[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-8)_[The Spectator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Spectator "The Spectator")_,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Spectator_UK-9)_[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-telegraph1-10) and _[Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington\_Post "Washington Post")_,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-11) it eschews the label.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Spectator_UK-9)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-12) Doon often draws attention, and sometimes criticism, from the media for the perceived disproportionate influence of its alumni in spheres such as Indian politics, business, or culture. In the 1980s, Prime Minister [Rajiv Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajiv_Gandhi "Rajiv Gandhi")'s administration was criticised, and labelled "Doon Cabinet", following the appointment of his school acquaintances to major posts. The school has educated a wide range of notable alumni, including politicians, diplomats, artists, writers and businesspeople including late Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and Olympic gold medalist [Abhinav Bindra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abhinav_Bindra "Abhinav Bindra").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-wsj-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-articles.economictimes.indiatimes.com-14)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Origins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origins")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/The_Doon_School_main_building_%28then_FRI%29_-_1917.jpg/330px-The_Doon_School_main_building_%28then_FRI%29_-_1917.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Doon_School_main_building_(then_FRI)_-_1917.jpg)

Main Building of Doon in 1917, when it was part of the [Forest Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Research_Institute_(India) "Forest Research Institute (India)").

Doon was the culmination of some considerable lobbying and efforts by [Satish Ranjan Das](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_Ranjan_Das "Satish Ranjan Das"), a lawyer from Calcutta and [advocate-general of Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advocate-General_of_Bengal "Advocate-General of Bengal"), who in 1927 became a member of the [Viceroy's Executive Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroy's_Executive_Council "Viceroy's Executive Council") of [Lord Irwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._F._L._Wood,_1st_Earl_of_Halifax "E. F. L. Wood, 1st Earl of Halifax").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-15) He envisioned a new kind of Indian public school that was modelled on traditional [British public schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_school_(United_Kingdom) "Public school (United Kingdom)"), but was "distinctively Indian in their moral and spiritual outlook and open to all castes and communities".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-16) While [Jawaharlal Nehru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru "Jawaharlal Nehru") welcomed the idea of such a school, there were many, like [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi") and [Rabindranath Tagore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore "Rabindranath Tagore"), who were opposed to it, considering it inegalitarian.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-18) Das travelled widely in India with the goal of collecting ₹40 million, but at the time of his death in 1928 had raised only ₹1 million in cash and a further ₹1 million in promises. With the money, Das formed the Indian Public Schools' Society (IPSS), with the objective of founding new public schools in India that would admit students regardless of caste, creed or social status.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-auto1-19)

After Das's death in 1928, the IPSS accomplished little, and by 1934 some of the original lenders had begun to inquire about the return of their money.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-auto1-19) To solve this problem, [Sir Joseph Bhore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._W._Bhore "J. W. Bhore"), then Railway Minister of [Lord Willingdon's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeman_Freeman-Thomas,_1st_Marquess_of_Willingdon "Freeman Freeman-Thomas, 1st Marquess of Willingdon") Council, became IPSS chairman, and along with [Sir Frank Noyce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Noyce "Frank Noyce") and [Sir Akbar Hydari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_Hydari "Akbar Hydari") as secretary, worked to obtain the former estate of the [Forest Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Research_Institute_(India) "Forest Research Institute (India)"), in [Dehradun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehradun "Dehradun"), from the government on favourable terms.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-20)[Lord Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._F._L._Wood,_1st_Earl_of_Halifax "E. F. L. Wood, 1st Earl of Halifax"), then President of the British Board of Education, led a selection committee that nominated [Arthur E. Foot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Foot "Arthur Foot"), a science teacher at [Eton College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eton_College "Eton College"), to be the first headmaster. The school admitted its first pupils on 10 September 1935, and on 27 October 1935, the [Viceroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroy "Viceroy"), [Lord Willingdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Willingdon "Lord Willingdon"), presided over the formal opening of the school. Seventy boys enrolled in the first term, and 110 more signed up for the second.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-21)

### Early years: 1935–1970

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early years: 1935–1970")]

Foot had never visited India before accepting the position of headmaster. He noted that the school appeared to be surrounded by forests and close to mountains, and the possibilities of outdoor recreation and mountaineering seem to have influenced his decision as much as the chance to create a completely new type of school in India.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-22) Foot's first action upon being offered the position was to recruit [J. A. K. (John) Martyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster) "John Martyn (schoolmaster)") from [Harrow School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrow_School "Harrow School") as his deputy. Although Martyn had not visited India before, he took up the offer because of the opportunity it afforded him to implement the ideas of German educator [Kurt Hahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Hahn "Kurt Hahn") at Doon; it was something he had not been able to do at Harrow.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-24) Doon's ethos and guiding principles were determined early in its life by Foot, Martyn, [R. L. Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._L._Holdsworth "R. L. Holdsworth") and [Jack Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Gibson_(schoolmaster) "Jack Gibson (schoolmaster)"), who went on to become principal of [Mayo College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayo_College "Mayo College"), and Martyn acknowledged the influence of Hahn's ideas in the development of the school's ethos.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-25) They were soon joined in their efforts by Indians such as the artist [Sudhir Khastgir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudhir_Khastgir "Sudhir Khastgir") (the school's first art teacher, who had trained previously in [Santiniketan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiniketan "Santiniketan")) and [Gurdial Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurdial_Singh_(mountaineer) "Gurdial Singh (mountaineer)"), a noted mountaineer who taught at Doon for several decades.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-26) In an essay entitled _The Objects of Education_ published in the school magazine, Foot offered a template for a complete education for boys, which included teaching them to form a habit of choosing good over evil, think logically, express their thoughts and views clearly, and maintain a healthy body.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-sixtyyears-27) At the opening of the school, he said, "Our boys should leave The Doon School as members of an aristocracy, but it must be an aristocracy of service inspired by the ideals of unselfishness, not one of privilege, wealth or position".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-29) The annual school fees in 1935 was ₹1,375, and by September 1946, had risen to ₹1,800.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-auto1-19) The [per-capita income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per-capita_income "Per-capita income") of India, then largely an agricultural society, in 1947 has been recorded as ₹252.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-30)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Arthur_Foot_and_Lord_Mountabatten_at_The_Doon_School.jpg/250px-Arthur_Foot_and_Lord_Mountabatten_at_The_Doon_School.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arthur_Foot_and_Lord_Mountabatten_at_The_Doon_School.jpg)

Arthur Foot and his daughter Sylvia Hartell with [Lord Mountbatten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mountbatten "Lord Mountbatten"), during the latter's visit to the school on 13 February 1948.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-31)

> ...By 14 he should have learnt all the ordinary principles of social behaviour. He should know how to stand up and speak to a variety of different types of people– to his own mother, to someone else's mother, to his father, to his schoolmasters, to servants, to Mahatma Gandhi or to the Viceroy, and to do this without any self-consciousness...At 17 must come another quality, less instinctive and requiring a maturer mind: he must acquire a capacity of judgement.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-sixtyyears-27)...

—Arthur Foot, 1946, _The Objects of Education_

In 1947, there were around 295 boys studying at Doon, out of which 58-69 were [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims"), 19-20 [Sikhs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikhs "Sikhs"), 11-24 [Parsees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsees "Parsees"), 6-7 Christians, and the remaining two-thirds Hindu.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-32) The first cohort of students left school in 1938, and during the Second World War, about 65 Doon students served in the [Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Army_during_World_War_II "Indian Army during World War II"), [Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Indian_Navy "Royal Indian Navy") or [Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Air_Force "Indian Air Force").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-33) In 1948, Foot returned to England for "unknown reasons", and John Martyn became the second headmaster.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Singh_2010_81-34) After the [Indian Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Independence_Act_1947 "Indian Independence Act 1947"), Martyn's friends suggested it would be a mistake to stay on in India, but he later wrote: "They could not have been more wrong. I have found my life much pleasanter than before...although no one had previously ever done or said anything to make me feel at all unwelcome, from now on it was often made quite explicit that I was very welcome."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Singh_2010_81-34) While Foot and Martyn were determined to model Doon on Eton and Harrow, they both agreed that Doon should cater primarily for Indian boys—and not the sons of British expatriates—in order to create a uniquely Indian public school rather than a transplanted British institution. Foot did not want Doon to be considered elitist. In a paper surveying the new school, presented to the [Royal Society of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_of_Arts "Royal Society of Arts"), London in 1947, Foot wrote: "In language we have never intended to base our instruction on the Classics in the way that Latin is still the centre pin of the English Public School. The great majority of boys take Urdu or Hindi."[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-35) Martyn retired as headmaster in 1966 and became a managing trustee of Indian [Cheshire Homes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire_Home "Cheshire Home").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-36)

The school's first Indian headmaster was [Eric Simeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Simeon "Eric Simeon"), appointed in 1970. He came from a military background and laid great emphasis on disciplined living.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-38) Simeon's tenure of nine years was marked with financial difficulties for the school and the estate suffered, as the funds were not enough to maintain buildings and facilities.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-39) In 1971, Simeon introduced the 'Scholar's Blazer', an academic equivalent of the pre-existing prize 'Games Blazer', so that boys accorded academic excellence the same level of prestige as they did sporting achievements.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Back_to_School-40) In 1979, [Gulab Ramchandani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulab_Ramchandani "Gulab Ramchandani") became the first alumnus to be appointed headmaster, and during his term the school regained financial stability.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-41) In 1988, [Shomie Das](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shomie_Das "Shomie Das"), another alumnus and the grandson of school founder Satish Ranjan Das, became headmaster. Das's focus was on upgrading the school infrastructure, and during his time the Oberoi house was added to the original four houses. The next headmaster, [John Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mason_(schoolmaster) "John Mason (schoolmaster)"), appointed in 1996, planned on making Doon more affordable to school pupils. The school did not raise its fees while Mason was in office.

#### Criticism of Rajiv Gandhi administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Criticism of Rajiv Gandhi administration")]

In the 1980s, the then [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_India "Prime Minister of India")[Rajiv Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajiv_Gandhi "Rajiv Gandhi"), an alumnus, drew criticism from the media for appointing many old boys to his administration.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-42) His inner circle was labelled a "Doon Cabinet"[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Spectator_UK-9) or "Dosco Mafia",[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-43) and _Washington Post_ reported,

> The catch phrase around Delhi these days is that the 'Doon School runs India,' but that is too simple an analysis for a complex, chaotic country with so many competing spheres of influence.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-bumiller1985-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-45)

Gandhi's reliance on Doon alumni for political advice later led Prime Minister [Morarji Desai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morarji_Desai "Morarji Desai") to remark, "If I had anything to do with this place, I'd close it down".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-bumiller1985-44) Although any alumnus seldom held public office for some time afterwards, this changed with the political ascendance of [Jyotiraditya Madhavrao Scindia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jyotiraditya_Scindia "Jyotiraditya Scindia"), [Naveen Patnaik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naveen_Patnaik "Naveen Patnaik"), and [Rahul Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahul_Gandhi "Rahul Gandhi").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-46)

### Recent years: 2000–present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Recent years: 2000–present")]

[Kanti Bajpai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanti_Bajpai "Kanti Bajpai") was the third old boy, after Gulab Ramchandani and Shomie Das, to become headmaster, when appointed to the post in 2003. He introduced numerous punishments, notably "yellow cards" (informally known as 'YCs'), to control an outburst of bullying at Doon.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-47) In 2006, Bajpai found himself embroiled in a controversy when the parents of Hindu and Sikh students complained on discovering that the school's dining hall only serves [halal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halal "Halal") meat.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-48) The fact came to light after a visiting Pakistani delegation was assured of their meal's halal status. Despite mounting pressure, the school's board of governors appealed for maintaining the status quo.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-49) As of 2016, the school was serving both halal and non-halal (_[jhatka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jhatka "Jhatka")_) meat varieties in the dining hall.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-50) In 2009, [Peter McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_McLaughlin "Peter McLaughlin"), an Irish academic, was chosen to lead the school, becoming the first non-Indian headmaster in almost four decades.

#### 2010 Founder's Day celebrations and film controversy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2010 Founder's Day celebrations and film controversy")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Doon_School_75th_Founder%27s_Day_-_DS75%2C_2010.jpg/330px-Doon_School_75th_Founder%27s_Day_-_DS75%2C_2010.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Doon_School_75th_Founder's_Day_-_DS75,_2010.jpg)

Main event at the 75th Founder's Day in October 2010, with chief guest President [Pratibha Patil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratibha_Patil "Pratibha Patil"), and other dignitaries including King of Bhutan [Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jigme_Khesar_Namgyel_Wangchuck "Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck"), Chief Minister [Ramesh Pokhriyal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramesh_Pokhriyal "Ramesh Pokhriyal"), Governor [Margaret Alva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Alva "Margaret Alva"), and Minister of Human Resource Development, [Kapil Sibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapil_Sibal "Kapil Sibal").

Founder's Day is a three-four day event in the autumn term, usually October, that marks the school's founding and draws many ex-pupils from all parts of the world.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-51) The chief guest is usually a prominent person, and the events include exhibitions, productions of plays, yoga sessions, live bands, a fete and an orchestral concert given by members of the school's Music Society.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-53) Doon celebrated its 75th Founder's Day in 2010 and programmed events on an unprecedented scale.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-hindustantimes.com-55) The event was christened _DS-75_.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Doon_school-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Founder's_Day_celebrations_to_begin_at_Doon_School-57) Among the chief guests were the then President of India [Pratibha Patil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratibha_Patil "Pratibha Patil"), King [Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jigme_Khesar_Namgyel_Wangchuck "Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck") of Bhutan, and [Kapil Sibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapil_Sibal "Kapil Sibal"), then minister of [Human Resource Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Human_Resource_Development_(India) "Ministry of Human Resource Development (India)").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-58) Pratibha Patil, in her address, urged the school authorities to make Doon a co-educational institution.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-telegraphindia1-59) One of the main events was a discussion, dubbed the "Chandbagh Debate", held between alumni including [Vikram Seth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vikram_Seth "Vikram Seth"), [Kamal Nath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamal_Nath "Kamal Nath"), [Manpreet Singh Badal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manpreet_Singh_Badal "Manpreet Singh Badal"), [Jyotiraditya Madhavrao Scindia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jyotiraditya_Madhavrao_Scindia "Jyotiraditya Madhavrao Scindia") and retired headmaster Kanti Bajpai, on the topic _Can India lead?_. It was moderated by television commentator [Karan Thapar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karan_Thapar "Karan Thapar"), an alumnus of the school.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-60)

[Ashvin Kumar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashvin_Kumar "Ashvin Kumar"), an alumnus and Oscar-nominated director, made the film _[Dazed in Doon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dazed\_in\_Doon "Dazed in Doon")_ for the celebrations, using pupils for the cast and crew. Most of it was shot in June and July during the summer break, and those scenes which required the entire student body were filmed after the school reopened in August.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-61) It was screened on the final day of celebrations to a gathering of over 2000 people, including guests, students, parents and alumni.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-62) The day after screening, the school objected to the film and its distribution, labelling the bullying scenes "defamatory", and obtained a court order to delay its release. The DVD sales on campus were immediately halted.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-fallout-63) The dispute remains unresolved between the director and school authorities.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-64) On 22 October 2010, a commemorative postage stamp depicting the school's main building was released by the [Indian Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Postal_Service "Indian Postal Service") to mark the occasion of the 75th Founder's Day.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-65)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Detail_of_The_Doon_School_Main_Gate.jpg/250px-Detail_of_The_Doon_School_Main_Gate.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Detail_of_The_Doon_School_Main_Gate.jpg)

In March 2020, the school closed for the first time since its founding, following the [COVID-19 outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_outbreak "COVID-19 outbreak").

#### Present day

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Present day")]

In June 2016, the school announced the appointment of [Matthew Raggett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Raggett "Matthew Raggett"), principal of the [Leipzig International School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig_International_School "Leipzig International School")'s secondary department, to succeed Peter McLaughlin as headmaster. Until the start of McLaughlin's headmastership, the student demographic was dominated by boys hailing from the [North Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Indian "North Indian") states.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-66) To make the school more diverse, Raggett continued McLaughlin's outreach initiative of inviting more applications from boys in [South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Indian "South Indian") and [Northeast Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_India "Northeast India") states.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-indiatimes2-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-68) The school was the subject of a 2018 [Channel 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_4 "Channel 4") documentary series called _[Indian Summer School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian\_Summer\_School "Indian Summer School")_, which was based on a social experiment to see if five under-performing British boys would thrive in Doon.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-69) In January 2020, Matthew Raggett stepped down as the tenth headmaster citing personal reasons. In March 2020, the school was shut down for the first time since its founding in 1935, and boys were sent home due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") and the [Indian lockdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdown_in_India "COVID-19 lockdown in India").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-70) Online classes were being conducted for students through video conferencing apps.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-71) Jagpreet Singh was appointed the eleventh headmaster of Doon in April 2020; he is a member of the [Headmasters' and Headmistresses' Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headmasters'_and_Headmistresses'_Conference "Headmasters' and Headmistresses' Conference"), UK.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-72)

## Governance and organisation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Governance and organisation")]

The school is owned by the [non-profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit "Non-profit") entity Indian Public Schools' Society (IPSS), which was registered by S.R. Das in 1928 with the aim of establishing public schools in India. Under the IPSS, the Board of Governors supervises all matters of Doon.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-73) The current board comprises thirteen members and is chaired by [Anoop Bishnoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anoop_Bishnoi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anoop Bishnoi (page does not exist)"), an alumnus. The president of [The Doon School Old Boys' Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School_Old_Boys'_Society "The Doon School Old Boys' Society") has a seat on the board to represent the views and interests of the alumni.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-auto2-74) At the intramural level, the School Council, comprising the headmaster, heads of department, staff and student representatives from each house, is responsible for legislating and discussing school policies. Every house holds a vote to send four student representatives to the council.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-75) Each house is run by a housemaster or a housemistress, along with a house captain and a team of [prefects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_prefect "School prefect"). The housemistress is assisted by a [matron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matron "Matron") known as "The Dame", who provides [pastoral care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoral_care "Pastoral care") for pupils, some of whom take several weeks to adjust fully to life in a boarding school, particularly given Doon's monastic lifestyle and strict routine.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-outlookindia2-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Futehally-77) The homes of housemasters and housemistresses are adjacent or physically attached to their houses to enable close supervision and support. One senior boy serves as [school captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_captain "School captain"), chosen by teachers and students at the start of the year by voting in a [secret ballot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_ballot "Secret ballot").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-78)

Doon follows the [house system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_system "House system"); there are five main houses (Hyderabad, Jaipur, Kashmir, Tata and Oberoi) and two 'holding houses' (Foot and Martyn, named after former headmasters), for boys in their first year.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Boarding_at_Doon-79) The four houses were named after the largest initial donors: Hyderabad House was named after [Akbar Hydari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar_Hydari "Akbar Hydari"), who secured a contribution from [Nizam of Hyderabad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nizam_of_Hyderabad "Nizam of Hyderabad")'s government; Kashmir, after [Maharajah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharajah "Maharajah")[Hari Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hari_Singh "Hari Singh"), then ruler of [Jammu and Kashmir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jammu_and_Kashmir_(princely_state) "Jammu and Kashmir (princely state)"); Tata, after the [Tata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tata_family "Tata family") Trusts; and Jaipur, after [Rai Bahadur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rai_Bahadur "Rai Bahadur") Amarnath Atal arranged for contributions from the [Durbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durbar_(court) "Durbar (court)") of [Jaipur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaipur "Jaipur").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-80) Boys are assigned to houses at the time of admission and develop great loyalty to them, since all [intramural sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intramural_sports "Intramural sports") involve fierce competition between houses. Those who have a family history with a particular house are assigned to the same house. All houses have rooms, dormitories, kitchen, library, study rooms, and a Common Room for recreation.

### Admission, fees and financial aid

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Admission, fees and financial aid")]

The school receives about 540 applications every year and admits 80 students in [seventh grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_grade "Seventh grade") and 14 in [eighth grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighth_grade "Eighth grade"), although these numbers have varied over time.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-81) Once admission is secured, after passing the entrance examination and interview, a student may apply for around 30 scholarships or bursaries. Some are reserved for boys proficient in sports or arts, and others for those from particular regions or the children of [armed forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces "Indian Armed Forces") personnel. As of August 2022, the annual school fees for Indian students was ₹11,20,000, and ₹14,00,000 for foreign nationals or [non-resident Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-resident_Indians "Non-resident Indians").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-82) The monetary value of financial aid ranges from fifty per cent of the tuition fee to being fully funded.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-83) Amidst criticism from parents over rising fees, the last headmaster, [Matthew Raggett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Raggett "Matthew Raggett"), has stated that over 25% of Doon's students receive needs-based bursaries, and the school is working towards a completely [needs-blind admission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need-blind_admission "Need-blind admission") policy.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-indiatimes2-67)

## Campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Campus")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Main_Field_at_The_Doon_School%2C_Dehradun%2C_India.jpg/500px-Main_Field_at_The_Doon_School%2C_Dehradun%2C_India.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Main_Field_at_The_Doon_School,_Dehradun,_India.jpg)

Main Field of the school with Hyderabad House in the background, and beyond, the [Mussoorie range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mussoorie "Mussoorie").

The school is spread across a single campus covering approximately 72 acres (290,000 m 2) flanked by Chakrata Road and Mall Road in the [Dehradun Cantonment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehradun_Cantonment "Dehradun Cantonment") area of Dehradun city, [Uttarakhand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uttarakhand "Uttarakhand"), India.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-wsj-13) To house the school, the IPSS acquired the Chandbagh Estate in Dehradun from the Uttar Pradesh Public Works Department on a 100-year lease of one rupee per year. This lease continues to date, having been since transferred to the [Indian Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces "Indian Armed Forces") overseeing the [Dehradun Cantonment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehradun_Cantonment "Dehradun Cantonment"). Part of the estate was once a deer park. The IPSS also acquired an adjoining estate, now known as Skinner's Field, from the descendants of [James Skinner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Skinner_(East_India_Company_officer) "James Skinner (East India Company officer)"). The buildings on campus include the Main Building, which houses offices and classrooms, structures for sports facilities, science blocks, music school, library, arts and media centre, auditorium, amphitheatre, dining hall, wellness centre, recycling and waste-treatment plants, and masters' residences.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-84)

### Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Rose_Bowl_amphitheatre%2C_The_Doon_School.jpg/250px-Rose_Bowl_amphitheatre%2C_The_Doon_School.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rose_Bowl_amphitheatre,_The_Doon_School.jpg)

The school's [amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphitheatre "Amphitheatre"), known as Rose Bowl, was constructed by the boys and masters in the early-1930s over two years. It was refurbished in 2009.

The construction of the Main Building, then in FRI, was carried out by Imperial Public Works Department, and finished in 1911. Its Renaissance-style architecture was inspired by [Basilica Palladiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_Palladiana "Basilica Palladiana") in [Vicenza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicenza "Vicenza"), Italy.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Fountain_Ink_essay-85) Many buildings on the campus have been designed by notable Indian architects or firms.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Architectural_Digest,_Doon_campus-86) The library was designed by Romi Khosla, the Biology block by Ram Sharma, teachers' residences by Anagram Architects, and the new Arts and Media Centre, which was inaugurated in October 2010 and shortlisted for the 2010 World Architecture News Education Award, by alumnus Sandeep Khosla [[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-88) The Arts and Media Centre houses painting, ceramic, sculpture, and textile studios, along with a lecture hall, film and photography studio, publications' room and exhibition galleries.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-89) In 2016, the school's Main Building received the "Honourable Mention" under the [UNESCO Asia-Pacific Awards for Cultural Heritage Conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO_Asia_Pacific_Heritage_Awards "UNESCO Asia Pacific Heritage Awards"), following the conservation work carried out by [Aishwarya Tipnis Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aishwarya_Tipnis_Architects "Aishwarya Tipnis Architects") on the more than a century-old building.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Architectural_Digest,_Doon_campus-86)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-90)

### Natural environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Natural environment")]

The school estate, known as Chandbagh (Urdu for "garden of the moon"),[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-91) lies in the green zone of the city and occupies the former site of the Imperial Forest Research Institute, now [Forest Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Research_Institute_(India) "Forest Research Institute (India)").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-92) Before the school's opening, the site had been the centre of forestry in India for three decades,[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-93) and, today, a wide variety of [flora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flora "Flora") and [fauna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna "Fauna") are found on campus, including many rare trees that date back to the days of the FRI.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Fountain_Ink_essay-85)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-wsj-13) The school has over 150 species of trees on its campus, and the formal gardens attract a variety of birds.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-94) The school is listed as a hotspot on the [eBird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EBird "EBird") database of [Cornell Lab of Ornithology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_Lab_of_Ornithology "Cornell Lab of Ornithology"), and 169 bird species had been identified on the campus as of February 2026.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-95) In the 1940–50s, ornithologist [Salim Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salim_Ali "Salim Ali"), who was a friend of Foot, Gibson and Martyn, was a regular visitor to the school; he sensitized generations of pupils to the natural diversity of the school campus, and introduced them to many aspects of ornithology.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-97) In 1996, a book titled _Trees of Chandbagh_ was released which provided a comprehensive account of vegetation found on Doon's campus.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-TreesofChandbagh-98) Along similar lines, the illustrated book _Birds of Chandbagh: A Guide To Birding at The Doon School_ was released in 2019, featuring photographs, illustrations and [QR codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_codes "QR codes") documenting the [bird calls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_calls "Bird calls") of the species found on campus.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-99) The school has devised an Architectural and Projects Committee, which ensures that any construction taking place on campus is done without disturbing the ecological balance of the wooded school grounds.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-100)

## Curriculum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Curriculum")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Main_Building_corridor_at_Doon_School.jpg/250px-Main_Building_corridor_at_Doon_School.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Main_Building_corridor_at_Doon_School.jpg)

Ground-floor corridor of the school's Main Building, which houses classrooms and offices.

The school practices a five-and-a-half-day week consisting of 40 periods (or "schools"), each of 40 minutes. The school day begins with boys having [chhota haazri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chhota_haazri "Chhota haazri") before doing [calisthenics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calisthenics "Calisthenics") outdoors on the playing fields, which is then followed by classes.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-101) On Sundays, boys are free to pursue any activity or sport. Senior boys may go into the town for leisure on designated Sundays, after taking permission from the housemaster of their respective houses.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Boarding_at_Doon-79) The student-teacher ratio at the school is 10:1.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-excellence-102) Doon pupils take the [International General Certificate of Secondary Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_General_Certificate_of_Secondary_Education "International General Certificate of Secondary Education") (IGCSE) exams in [tenth grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenth_grade "Tenth grade"), which replaced [Indian Certificate of Secondary Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Certificate_of_Secondary_Education "Indian Certificate of Secondary Education") in 2017, and are thereafter offered two strands for the final two years: [International Baccalaureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Baccalaureate "International Baccalaureate") (IB) or [Indian School Certificate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_School_Certificate "Indian School Certificate") (ISC).[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-autogenerated2006-103)

The academic year has three terms: spring, summer and autumn. The autumn term runs from August to the year-end final examinations in November, after which the boys are promoted to the new class in February.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-104) Each term has a "test week" and end-of-term examinations known as "trials". Boys are able to visit teachers, most of whom live on campus, for further academic help. Additionally, each boy is assigned a 'Tutor' – a School Master affiliated with their boarding house – who is responsible for their pastoral welfare and may coordinate academic help when requested. Subjects on offer include geography, political science, history, economics, accountancy, commerce, environmental studies, art and design, psychology, music, English, Hindi, Sanskrit and [STEM subjects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STEM_subjects "STEM subjects"). Doon's foreign language offerings include French, German and Spanish. The school's Careers Information, Education and Guidance Department has offered pupils guidance on career paths, college applications, entrance exams and standardized tests like the [SAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAT "SAT") and [ACT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_(test) "ACT (test)"). In recent years, boys have increasingly chosen foreign universities over Indian colleges, sometimes due to the hyper-competitiveness of the [Indian higher education system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education_in_India "Higher education in India") that calls for extremely high school-leaving scores for admissions.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-auto2-74)

### Traditions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Traditions")]

The early headmasters and teachers at Doon came from traditional British public schools, and the jargon introduced by them is still in use. For example, the weekly masters' meeting, started by Foot, is called _Chambers_, a term taken from Eton, and evening "prep" (the boarding-school equivalent of homework) is called _toye-time_, a term taken from [Winchester College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester_College "Winchester College").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-106) The school songs were deliberately chosen to include both [Urdu poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urdu_poetry "Urdu poetry") and Hindu [bhajans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhajan "Bhajan") as a way of emphasising Doon's secular ethos; similarly, the school prayers include a mix of Anglican hymns and Indian poetry representing different geo-linguistic regions of the country.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-107) Attendance at the morning assembly is required of all pupils and teachers. It traditionally begins with a song from the school's song book, which contains poetry, hymns and [bhajans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhajans "Bhajans"), including _[Jana Gana Mana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jana\_Gana\_Mana "Jana Gana Mana")_ by [Rabindranath Tagore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore "Rabindranath Tagore"), _Chisti Ne Jis Zamin Mein_ by [Muhammad Iqbal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Iqbal "Muhammad Iqbal"), _Anand Loke_ by [Rabindranath Tagore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore "Rabindranath Tagore"), _[Lab Pe Aati Hai Dua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lab\_Pe\_Aati\_Hai\_Dua "Lab Pe Aati Hai Dua")_ by Muhammad Iqbal, _Ghungat Ke Pat Khol Re_ (attributed to [Meerabai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meerabai "Meerabai")), _[Vande Mataram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vande\_Mataram "Vande Mataram")_ (from a poem by [Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankim_Chandra_Chattopadhyay "Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay")). Although _[Jana Gana Mana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jana\_Gana\_Mana "Jana Gana Mana")_ is India's [national anthem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_anthem "National anthem"), it is traditionally referred to as "Song No. 1" at Doon since it was adopted as the school song in 1935, fifteen years before it became India's national anthem.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-108) Social work, known formally as "Socially Useful Productive Work" (SUPW), is also part of school life. All boys of the school must complete a mandatory quota of social service hours every term, which is also required by both curricula offered at the school (the International Baccalaureate referring to this as Creativity, Activity and Service or 'CAS').[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-109) Though, previously, students that didn't complete their hours of work were required to stay back at school over the holidays for a brief period, this has been relaxed in recent years. Doon also oversees a Panchayat Ghar (or 'village house') teaching impoverished children, and many building projects and workshops for the local community. Pupils and alumni have frequently helped local villages of organised efforts across India to assist people affected by natural disasters.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-110) During the [1991 Uttarkashi earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Uttarkashi_earthquake "1991 Uttarkashi earthquake"), the school's amateur radio club was used by the government for communication purposes.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-111)

## Extracurricular activities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Extracurricular activities")]

### Sports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Sports")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Cricket_at_The_Doon_School.jpg/250px-Cricket_at_The_Doon_School.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cricket_at_The_Doon_School.jpg)

A cricket game in progress on the Main Field.

Sports are compulsory for pupils. The school has over 30 acres (120,000 m 2) of playing fields, the largest of which are Skinner Field and the Main Field. Cricket and hockey dominate the sports calendar in spring term, while football, athletics and boxing are played in autumn term. Other sports such as tennis, table tennis, badminton, squash, basketball, swimming and gymnastics are played all-year round. Inter-house matches are played in cricket, hockey, football, boxing and basketball. Sports facilities include a 25-metre swimming pool, a boxing ring and a multi-purpose hall with a gymnasium, yoga studio, and facilities for indoor badminton, basketball and table tennis. There are two [artificial turf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_turf "Artificial turf") cricket pitches, five basketball courts, four tennis courts, four squash courts, eight cricket nets, seven fields for hockey and football (which can be converted to four cricket pitches to accommodate seasonal sports), a modern cricket pavilion and two 400-metre athletics tracks. In 2014, the school inaugurated a shooting range on campus. [Golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf "Golf") is offered to boys in partnership with local golf courses.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-112) Doon hosts the annual Afzal Khan Memorial Basketball Tournament, an inter-school tournament that draws all major school basketball teams of India.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-113)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-114)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-115) Boys visit other schools and academies from time to time to take part in various tournaments. For skill improvement, the school often invites professional sports bodies to hold training camps, which are usually open to students from across India. In 2013, a football coaching camp was held in association with Barça Academy, the official training school of [FC Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Barcelona "FC Barcelona"),[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-116) and in January 2015, coaches from the [Marylebone Cricket Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marylebone_Cricket_Club "Marylebone Cricket Club") held a week-long cricket training camp on the school grounds.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-117)

### Clubs and societies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Clubs and societies")]

Further information: [The Doon School Model United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School_Model_United_Nations "The Doon School Model United Nations")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/The_Doon_School_Weekly.jpg/250px-The_Doon_School_Weekly.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Doon_School_Weekly.jpg)

_[The Doon School Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Doon\_School\_Weekly "The Doon School Weekly")_, established in 1936, is the oldest publication of Doon. It is produced by the boys and distributed every Saturday morning.

Extracurricular activities are also a compulsory element of school life. There are around 70-80 clubs and societies, including astronomy, business, [The Doon School Model United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School_Model_United_Nations "The Doon School Model United Nations"), quiz, photography and film, [aeromodelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_aircraft "Model aircraft"), robotics, paper recycling, weather reporting, pottery, carpentry, [amateur radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_radio "Amateur radio") (school [call sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_signs_in_India "Call signs in India"): VU2CHC) and birdwatching, among others.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-118) In many societies pupils come together to discuss a particular topic, presided over by a schoolmaster and often including a guest speaker. The school has often invited prominent figures to give speeches and talks to the students; these have included heads of state, politicians, ornithologists, naturalists, artists, writers, economists, diplomats and industrialists.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-119)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-120)

Boys can write for, or join the editorial board of, a number of school magazines that are published in English or Hindi. _[The Doon School Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Doon\_School\_Weekly "The Doon School Weekly")_, established in 1936, is the oldest publication and the official school newspaper.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-121) Distributed every Saturday morning, and edited by pupils, it chronicles school activities and is a platform for creative, political or humorous writing.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-122) The publication aims to represent the views of the school community as well as Old Boys, and include satire and criticism of school policies. More subversive publications, critical of teachers and the school establishment, have occasionally been produced without official sponsorship. Other magazines include _The Yearbook_, a heavily illustrated publication for recording all highlights of the school year, and _The Doon School Information Review_ for cultural criticism. Specialist publications by academic departments include _Vibgyor_ (Art), _Echo_ (Science), _The Econocrat_ (Economics), _Infinity_ (Mathematics), _Grand Slam_ (Sports) and _The Circle_ (History and Political Science).[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-123)

### Trekking and mountaineering

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Trekking and mountaineering")]

Main article: [Role of The Doon School in Indian mountaineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Role_of_The_Doon_School_in_Indian_mountaineering "Role of The Doon School in Indian mountaineering")

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Mt._Everest_Base_Camp_Expedition_-_2008%2C_The_Doon_School.jpg/250px-Mt._Everest_Base_Camp_Expedition_-_2008%2C_The_Doon_School.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mt._Everest_Base_Camp_Expedition_-_2008,_The_Doon_School.jpg)

2008 expedition to the [Mount Everest Base Camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest_Base_Camp "Mount Everest Base Camp") and [Kala Patthar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kala_Patthar "Kala Patthar").

Halfway through each term, the boys go on a one-week "midterm", an expedition through the [Siwalik Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siwalik_Hills "Siwalik Hills") or [Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas"). Senior boys make treks of up to five days, unaccompanied by teachers, camping out in tents and cooking their own food. The trips are planned by students themselves. Alumni have recalled these midterms as formative and character-building experiences.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-wsj-13)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-124) Doon has been credited with pioneering mountaineering in India, due to the accomplishments of masters such as [R. L. Holdsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._L._Holdsworth "R. L. Holdsworth"), [Jack Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Gibson_(schoolmaster) "Jack Gibson (schoolmaster)") and [Gurdial Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurdial_Singh_(mountaineer) "Gurdial Singh (mountaineer)"), and alumni like [Nandu Jayal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Dhar_Jayal "Narendra Dhar Jayal"), who later became the founder principal of [Himalayan Mountaineering Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayan_Mountaineering_Institute "Himalayan Mountaineering Institute").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Kohli-125) Notable climbs by staff and alumni include [Bandarpunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandarpunch "Bandarpunch") (6,316 m) in 1950, Kala Nag (6,387 m) in 1956, [Trisul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trisul "Trisul") (7,120 m) in 1951, [Kamet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamet "Kamet") (7,756 m) in 1955, [Abi Gamin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abi_Gamin "Abi Gamin") (7,355 m) in 1953 and 1955, Mrigthuni (6,855 m) in 1958 and Jaonli (6,632 metres) in 1964.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-126) Some of these expeditions have been noted for their idiosyncrasies. After Gurdial Singh led a successful climb of Trisul, he performed a headstand [asana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asana "Asana") on the summit as a tribute to the Hindu god [Shiva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiva "Shiva"), who is said to abide there. Holdsworth smoked a pipe on reaching the summit of Kamet (7,756 m), during its first ascent in 1931.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-Harish_Kapadia-127) Two Doon pupils climbed the [Matterhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matterhorn "Matterhorn") in 1951 wearing cricket boots.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-alpinejournal-128)

### Theatre and music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Theatre and music")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Waiting_for_Godot_in_Doon_School.jpg/250px-Waiting_for_Godot_in_Doon_School.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Waiting_for_Godot_in_Doon_School.jpg)

[Samuel Beckett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Beckett "Samuel Beckett")'s _[Waiting for Godot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waiting\_for\_Godot "Waiting for Godot")_ being staged in the open-air theatre, Rose Bowl.

An [amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphitheatre "Amphitheatre") known as the Rose Bowl was built largely by pupils and masters in two years during the 1930s[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-wsj-13)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-129) and underwent a major structural change in 2009.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-130) It can seat up to 2,000 people and has been the setting for numerous plays as well as musical performances and speeches during school ceremonies such as Founder's Day.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-131) The Multi-Purpose Hall is a more modern indoor theatre that can accommodate approximately 2,000 people. Plays are regularly staged in English and Hindi, with 8–9 productions each year including 2 major productions, which usually have a larger cast and budget, as part of the Founder's Day celebrations. The Inter House Once-Act Play competition is held each year, alternatively in English and Hindi. The [stage design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_design "Stage design"), [sound design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_design "Sound design"), stage lighting, and much of the set construction are the responsibility of the pupils.

In 2001, a new music school was built beside the Rose Bowl. It houses a [music library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_library "Music library"), a [concert hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert_hall "Concert hall") and several practice and teaching rooms where students learn various western and Indian instruments.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-132) Pupils of the school have an option to appear for the [Trinity Guildhall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Guildhall "Trinity Guildhall") music examinations, conducted by [Trinity College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College_London "Trinity College London"), in piano, violin, drums and classical guitar. In 2002, the school choir raised ₹2 million for victims of the [2001 Gujarat earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Gujarat_earthquake "2001 Gujarat earthquake") by organising a charity concert with the title _Concerto 2000_, in which drummer [Sivamani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sivamani_(percussionist) "Sivamani (percussionist)") also took part.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-133)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-134) To commemorate its 75th Founder's Day in 2010, the school launched a music album, called _Spirit of Doon_ in collaboration with [EMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMI "EMI"). The tracks were written by the lyricist [Gulzar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulzar "Gulzar") and were sung by the school choir, [Sonu Nigam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonu_Nigam "Sonu Nigam"), Shayan Italia and [Bhajan Sopori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhajan_Sopori "Bhajan Sopori").[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-bare_url-135)

## Affiliations and partnerships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Affiliations and partnerships")]

From its foundation in 1937 until the early 1980s, [Welham Boys' School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welham_Boys'_School "Welham Boys' School") was a [feeder school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feeder_school "Feeder school") for Doon School and Mayo College.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-136) This ended when Surendra Kandhari, an old boy and former housemaster at Doon, became principal of Welham and transformed it into a high school. Families who send their sons to Doon often send their daughters to [Welham Girls' School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welham_Girls'_School "Welham Girls' School"), and many Doon alumni have married alumnae of Welham.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-137) The two schools hold an annual "dance social", and their alumni sometimes collaborate in organising events. Pakistani ex-pupils from Doon established the [Chand Bagh School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chand_Bagh_School "Chand Bagh School") 40 km north of [Lahore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore "Lahore"), Pakistan, in 1998, modelling it on the general structure of Doon.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-138)

Doon also has exchange programmes with a number of overseas schools, such as Eton College, Harrow School and St Edward's School, Oxford, [St. Albans School, Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Albans_School_(Washington,_D.C.) ### Schools with similar names

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Doon_School&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Schools with similar names")]

As private schools became more widespread in India, several other schools used "Doon" as part of their names, causing some confusion.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-148) Among them are Doon Global School, Doon Presidency School, Doon International School, Doon Preparatory School, Doon Cambridge School, Doon Girls School, Doon Public School (in West Delhi, not the Doon Valley) Doon Heritage School (Siliguri, West Bengal) and the Doon College of Spoken English. None of them are related to The Doon School.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doon_School#cite_note-indiatimes1-149) Former Headmaster Peter McLaughlin had, during his tenure, sought to copyright the school's name and initiate legal proceedings against institutions falsely presenting themselves as connected to the school, but was unsuccessful.

**John A. K. Martyn**[OBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") (more commonly known as **J. A. K. Martyn**) (1903–1984), was an English [schoolmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schoolmaster "Schoolmaster"), scholar, academic and a distinguished British [Himalayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalaya "Himalaya")[mountaineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineer "Mountaineer"). He was the second headmaster of The Doon School.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1935, John Martyn accompanied [Arthur Foot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Foot "Arthur Foot") to India to establish the teaching staff of The Doon School, a newly opened [boarding school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boarding_school "Boarding school") for Indian boys.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-2)

Martyn had previously taught at [Harrow School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrow_School "Harrow School") in England for ten years before he moved to India.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-3) In Doon, he was given the post of Deputy Headmaster, which he kept till 1948. Shortly after Indian independence in 1947, Foot left [Dehradun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehradun "Dehradun") to take up the headship of [Ottershaw School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottershaw_School "Ottershaw School"), and Martyn succeeded him to become the second headmaster of the Doon School.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-4) Martyn was at Doon for 31 years, thus becoming one of the longest-serving schoolmasters in the school's history. Of those 31 years, 18 were spent as Headmaster, making him the school's longest-serving Headmaster to date.

Apart from teaching, Martyn was very keen on mountaineering, and was part of the expedition team to [Trisul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trisul "Trisul") with pioneers like [Jack Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Gibson_(schoolmaster) "Jack Gibson (schoolmaster)"), [Gurdial Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurdial_Singh_(mountaineer) "Gurdial Singh (mountaineer)") and [Nandu Jayal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandu_Jayal "Nandu Jayal").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-7) He, along with Jack Gibson, climbed [Bandarpunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandarpunch "Bandarpunch") with [Tenzing Norgay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenzing_Norgay "Tenzing Norgay"), who later became the first man to climb [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-8)

## Honours and distinctions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Honours and distinctions")]

Martyn was appointed an Officer of the [Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") by [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") in 1958, and in 1983 [Padma Shri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Shri "Padma Shri"), the fourth-highest civilian award in India, from the [Government of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India "Government of India") for his notable contributions to the establishment of the Doon School.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-9) He was one of the few Englishmen to have been honoured by both the governments.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-10) He was also a member of the famed [Alpine Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_Club "Alpine Club").

After his death in 1984, his wife Mady Martyn wrote a book about him entitled _Martyn Sahib, the story of John Martyn of the Doon School_. In his honour, his wife and Martyn's friends set up _John Martyn Memorial Trust_ in a village at the foothills of [Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas") called Salangaon. The trust runs a school for underprivileged children and provides free education to over 150 children.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-11)

Martyn House, a holding-house for new students at Doon, was named after him.

**John A. K. Martyn**[OBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") (more commonly known as **J. A. K. Martyn**) (1903–1984), was an English [schoolmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schoolmaster "Schoolmaster"), scholar, academic and a distinguished British [Himalayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalaya "Himalaya")[mountaineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineer "Mountaineer"). He was the second headmaster of The Doon School.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1935, John Martyn accompanied [Arthur Foot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Foot "Arthur Foot") to India to establish the teaching staff of The Doon School, a newly opened [boarding school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boarding_school "Boarding school") for Indian boys.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-2)

Martyn had previously taught at [Harrow School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrow_School "Harrow School") in England for ten years before he moved to India.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-3) In Doon, he was given the post of Deputy Headmaster, which he kept till 1948. Shortly after Indian independence in 1947, Foot left [Dehradun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehradun "Dehradun") to take up the headship of [Ottershaw School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottershaw_School "Ottershaw School"), and Martyn succeeded him to become the second headmaster of the Doon School.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-4) Martyn was at Doon for 31 years, thus becoming one of the longest-serving schoolmasters in the school's history. Of those 31 years, 18 were spent as Headmaster, making him the school's longest-serving Headmaster to date.

Apart from teaching, Martyn was very keen on mountaineering, and was part of the expedition team to [Trisul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trisul "Trisul") with pioneers like [Jack Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Gibson_(schoolmaster) "Jack Gibson (schoolmaster)"), [Gurdial Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurdial_Singh_(mountaineer) "Gurdial Singh (mountaineer)") and [Nandu Jayal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandu_Jayal "Nandu Jayal").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-7) He, along with Jack Gibson, climbed [Bandarpunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandarpunch "Bandarpunch") with [Tenzing Norgay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenzing_Norgay "Tenzing Norgay"), who later became the first man to climb [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-8)

## Honours and distinctions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Honours and distinctions")]

Martyn was appointed an Officer of the [Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") by [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") in 1958, and in 1983 [Padma Shri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Shri "Padma Shri"), the fourth-highest civilian award in India, from the [Government of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India "Government of India") for his notable contributions to the establishment of the Doon School.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-9) He was one of the few Englishmen to have been honoured by both the governments.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-10) He was also a member of the famed [Alpine Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_Club "Alpine Club").

After his death in 1984, his wife Mady Martyn wrote a book about him entitled _Martyn Sahib, the story of John Martyn of the Doon School_. In his honour, his wife and Martyn's friends set up _John Martyn Memorial Trust_ in a village at the foothills of [Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas") called Salangaon. The trust runs a school for underprivileged children and provides free education to over 150 children.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._A._K._Martyn#cite_note-11)

Martyn House, a holding-house for new students at Doon, was named after him.
