**John A. K. Martyn**[OBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") (more commonly known as **J. A. K. Martyn**) (1903–1984), was an English [schoolmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schoolmaster "Schoolmaster"), scholar, academic and a distinguished British [Himalayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalaya "Himalaya")[mountaineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineer "Mountaineer"). He was the second headmaster of The Doon School.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1935, John Martyn accompanied [Arthur Foot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Foot "Arthur Foot") to India to establish the teaching staff of The Doon School, a newly opened [boarding school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boarding_school "Boarding school") for Indian boys.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-2)

Martyn had previously taught at [Harrow School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrow_School "Harrow School") in England for ten years before he moved to India.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-3) In Doon, he was given the post of Deputy Headmaster, which he kept till 1948. Shortly after Indian independence in 1947, Foot left [Dehradun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehradun "Dehradun") to take up the headship of [Ottershaw School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottershaw_School "Ottershaw School"), and Martyn succeeded him to become the second headmaster of the Doon School.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-4) Martyn was at Doon for 31 years, thus becoming one of the longest-serving schoolmasters in the school's history. Of those 31 years, 18 were spent as Headmaster, making him the school's longest-serving Headmaster to date.

Apart from teaching, Martyn was very keen on mountaineering, and was part of the expedition team to [Trisul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trisul "Trisul") with pioneers like [Jack Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Gibson_(schoolmaster) "Jack Gibson (schoolmaster)"), [Gurdial Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurdial_Singh_(mountaineer) "Gurdial Singh (mountaineer)") and [Nandu Jayal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandu_Jayal "Nandu Jayal").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-7) He, along with Jack Gibson, climbed [Bandarpunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandarpunch "Bandarpunch") with [Tenzing Norgay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenzing_Norgay "Tenzing Norgay"), who later became the first man to climb [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-8)

## Honours and distinctions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Honours and distinctions")]

Martyn was appointed an Officer of the [Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") by [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") in 1958, and in 1983 [Padma Shri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Shri "Padma Shri"), the fourth-highest civilian award in India, from the [Government of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India "Government of India") for his notable contributions to the establishment of the Doon School.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-9) He was one of the few Englishmen to have been honoured by both the governments.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-10) He was also a member of the famed [Alpine Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_Club "Alpine Club").

After his death in 1984, his wife Mady Martyn wrote a book about him entitled _Martyn Sahib, the story of John Martyn of the Doon School_. In his honour, his wife and Martyn's friends set up _John Martyn Memorial Trust_ in a village at the foothills of [Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas") called Salangaon. The trust runs a school for underprivileged children and provides free education to over 150 children.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-11)

Martyn House, a holding-house for new students at Doon, was named after him.

**John A. K. Martyn**[OBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") (more commonly known as **J. A. K. Martyn**) (1903–1984), was an English [schoolmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schoolmaster "Schoolmaster"), scholar, academic and a distinguished British [Himalayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalaya "Himalaya")[mountaineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineer "Mountaineer"). He was the second headmaster of The Doon School.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

In 1935, John Martyn accompanied [Arthur Foot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Foot "Arthur Foot") to India to establish the teaching staff of The Doon School, a newly opened [boarding school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boarding_school "Boarding school") for Indian boys.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-2)

Martyn had previously taught at [Harrow School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrow_School "Harrow School") in England for ten years before he moved to India.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-3) In Doon, he was given the post of Deputy Headmaster, which he kept till 1948. Shortly after Indian independence in 1947, Foot left [Dehradun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehradun "Dehradun") to take up the headship of [Ottershaw School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottershaw_School "Ottershaw School"), and Martyn succeeded him to become the second headmaster of the Doon School.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-4) Martyn was at Doon for 31 years, thus becoming one of the longest-serving schoolmasters in the school's history. Of those 31 years, 18 were spent as Headmaster, making him the school's longest-serving Headmaster to date.

Apart from teaching, Martyn was very keen on mountaineering, and was part of the expedition team to [Trisul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trisul "Trisul") with pioneers like [Jack Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Gibson_(schoolmaster) "Jack Gibson (schoolmaster)"), [Gurdial Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurdial_Singh_(mountaineer) "Gurdial Singh (mountaineer)") and [Nandu Jayal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandu_Jayal "Nandu Jayal").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-7) He, along with Jack Gibson, climbed [Bandarpunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandarpunch "Bandarpunch") with [Tenzing Norgay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenzing_Norgay "Tenzing Norgay"), who later became the first man to climb [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-8)

## Honours and distinctions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Honours and distinctions")]

Martyn was appointed an Officer of the [Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") by [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") in 1958, and in 1983 [Padma Shri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Shri "Padma Shri"), the fourth-highest civilian award in India, from the [Government of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India "Government of India") for his notable contributions to the establishment of the Doon School.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-9) He was one of the few Englishmen to have been honoured by both the governments.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-10) He was also a member of the famed [Alpine Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_Club "Alpine Club").

After his death in 1984, his wife Mady Martyn wrote a book about him entitled _Martyn Sahib, the story of John Martyn of the Doon School_. In his honour, his wife and Martyn's friends set up _John Martyn Memorial Trust_ in a village at the foothills of [Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas") called Salangaon. The trust runs a school for underprivileged children and provides free education to over 150 children.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Martyn_(schoolmaster)#cite_note-11)

Martyn House, a holding-house for new students at Doon, was named after him.

![Image 5](https://www.doonschool.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/srdas.jpg)

The Doon School was founded in 1935 by S. R. Das, a lawyer from Calcutta, who later served as the Advocate General of Bengal and was a member of the Viceroy’s Executive Council of Lord Irwin. Inspired by his experience as a student at the prestigious Manchester Grammar School in England, he returned to India with a vision to establish an institute founded on the model of British private boarding schools while remaining deeply anchored in the Indian identity and heritage. The Doon School was envisioned as an entirely secular school that would attract boys from all sections of Indian society and from every state in India; boys who would go on to serve a free and democratic India.

The first Headmaster was Arthur Foot, a science master from Eton College. His deputy, John Martyn, who was a Housemaster from Harrow, later became the second Headmaster of the school. On the school’s inaugural Founder’s Day, Arthur Foot proclaimed what would become the guiding philosophy of The Doon School:

_“The boys should leave The Doon School as members of an aristocracy, but it must be an aristocracy of service inspired by the ideals of unselfishness, not one of privilege, wealth or position.”_

Today, The Doon School continues to uphold the founding ideals laid down by its founders. Conceived as an all-boarding institution in 1935, the school has grown into a vibrant residential community of around 600 boys aged 12 to 18, housed in five main boarding houses and two holding houses.
